title: ADAPT 2-Hour Accelerated Diagnostic Protocol
reference: Than M et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2014;174(1):51–58. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2013.11362
the_hook: A randomized implementation trial of a 2-hour accelerated diagnostic pathway using modified TIMI score 0, ECG, and 0- and 2-hour contemporary troponin testing.
if_consultant_asks: The experimental pathway nearly doubled successful discharge within 6 hours. The randomized trial used a contemporary troponin I assay, not a high-sensitivity assay, and included outpatient stress testing within 72 hours.
killer_stat: Successful discharge occurred in 19.3% versus 11.0% (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.18–3.13; p=0.008). One low-risk experimental-pathway patient had a 30-day MACE, giving an NPV of 98.9%, not 100%.
shift_action: Use only within a locally approved ACS pathway that matches the troponin assay, eligibility criteria, serial-testing interval, and follow-up capacity used by the service.
review_note: Retained the v3 correction: the randomized trial used a contemporary, not high-sensitivity, troponin assay and did not achieve a 100% NPV. Removed opaque bracket citations.

title: REASON-1
reference: Gaspari R et al. Resuscitation. 2016;109:33–39. doi:10.1016/j.resuscitation.2016.09.018
the_hook: A prospective, multicentre observational study of point-of-care cardiac ultrasound during out-of-hospital and emergency-department cardiac arrest.
if_consultant_asks: Cardiac activity on ultrasound was strongly associated with ROSC and survival, and ultrasound sometimes identified reversible causes. This was association, not proof that ultrasound-guided termination improves outcomes.
killer_stat: Among 793 patients, absence of cardiac activity was associated with poor outcome, but 0.6% (95% CI 0.3–2.3%) still survived to discharge.
shift_action: Use POCUS during planned rhythm checks without prolonging compression pauses and to seek reversible causes. Do not use cardiac standstill as the sole reason to terminate resuscitation.
review_note: Corrected the v3 type from clinical trial to observational study and retained its warning against ultrasound-only termination decisions.

title: The SPARC Trial
reference: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07002294
the_hook: An ongoing randomized trial of specialty post-arrest care following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
if_consultant_asks: SPARC is evaluating whether an organized specialty-care strategy improves recovery after cardiac arrest. The registry describes the planned comparison; it does not provide an efficacy result.
killer_stat: No primary outcome result is available while the trial remains ongoing.
shift_action: Do not change destination or post-arrest treatment on the basis of this ongoing trial. Follow the regional referral pathway and current local protocol.
review_note: The v3 ongoing status is retained. No unpublished outcome or implied benefit is presented.

title: ACT-GLOBAL
reference: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06352632
the_hook: An active international adaptive platform trial evaluating multiple treatment domains across stroke states.
if_consultant_asks: ACT-GLOBAL uses a master protocol and domain-specific registrations so interventions can enter or leave the platform as evidence accumulates.
killer_stat: No platform-level treatment result is available; individual domains have their own enrollment and completion timelines.
shift_action: Follow current stroke protocols. Consider trial enrollment only through an approved participating site and domain-specific consent pathway.
review_note: The v3 ongoing status is retained. The card does not imply that the platform has established treatment efficacy.

title: PARAMEDIC-2
reference: Perkins GD et al. N Engl J Med. 2018;379:711–721. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1806842
the_hook: A double-blind randomized comparison of epinephrine and placebo in adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
if_consultant_asks: Epinephrine increased 30-day survival, but the trial did not find a significant improvement in survival with favourable neurologic outcome; more survivors in the epinephrine group had severe neurologic impairment.
killer_stat: Thirty-day survival was 3.2% with epinephrine versus 2.4% with placebo (unadjusted OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.06–1.82; p=0.02).
shift_action: Follow the locally approved adult cardiac-arrest algorithm. This trial informs benefit–harm discussions but does not by itself replace current resuscitation guidance.
review_note: Moved the v3 card out of the sepsis domain and removed wording that treated a trial result as a universal drug instruction.

title: PARAMEDIC-3
reference: Couper K et al. N Engl J Med. 2025;392:336–348. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2407780 (online 2024)
the_hook: A multicentre randomized comparison of intraosseous-first and intravenous-first vascular-access strategies during adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
if_consultant_asks: An IO-first strategy did not improve 30-day survival compared with an IV-first strategy. IO achieved assigned-route access more often, but ROSC was lower and neurologically favourable survival was similar.
killer_stat: Thirty-day survival was 4.5% with IO-first versus 5.1% with IV-first (adjusted OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.68–1.32; p=0.74).
shift_action: Do not infer that IO is ineffective or prohibited: use the locally approved vascular-access sequence, with IO as a rapid alternative when IV access is not promptly achievable.
review_note: Replaced the v3's qualitative result with the published estimate and confidence interval; the trial did not establish equivalence.

title: CRASH-2
the_hook: A large international randomized trial of tranexamic acid versus placebo in adult trauma patients with, or at risk of, significant bleeding.
if_consultant_asks: Tranexamic acid reduced all-cause and bleeding mortality without a significant increase in vascular occlusive events in the primary trial. A prespecified exploratory analysis found the benefit was time-dependent and treatment after 3 hours appeared harmful.
killer_stat: All-cause mortality was 14.5% with tranexamic acid versus 16.0% with placebo (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85–0.97; p=0.0035).
shift_action: Use tranexamic acid only for patients meeting the locally approved trauma criteria and as early as possible within the protocol's time window; do not extrapolate the trial to late or non-bleeding presentations.
review_note: Changed the v3's categorical 'actually increases' wording to reflect that the after-3-hour harm signal came from an exploratory time-to-treatment analysis.

title: CRASH-3
the_hook: An international randomized placebo-controlled trial of tranexamic acid in adults with acute traumatic brain injury treated within 3 hours.
if_consultant_asks: The primary analysis did not show a statistically significant reduction in head-injury death overall. Prespecified analyses suggested benefit in less severe injury and little prospect of benefit in patients with GCS 3 or bilateral unreactive pupils.
killer_stat: Head-injury death was 18.5% with tranexamic acid versus 19.8% with placebo (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.86–1.02); after excluding GCS 3 or bilateral unreactive pupils, RR was 0.89 (95% CI 0.80–1.00).
shift_action: Use the locally approved traumatic-brain-injury protocol and eligibility window. Do not present the mild-to-moderate subgroup finding as a statistically positive overall primary result.
review_note: Corrected the v3 claim that CRASH-3 broadly proved a mortality reduction; the overall primary result was not statistically significant.

title: ProCESS
reference: ProCESS Investigators. N Engl J Med. 2014;370:1683–1693. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1401602
the_hook: A multicentre three-group randomized trial comparing protocol-based EGDT, protocol-based standard therapy, and usual care for early septic shock.
if_consultant_asks: Protocol-based care, including invasive EGDT targets, did not improve survival over contemporary usual care.
killer_stat: Sixty-day in-hospital mortality was 21.0% with protocol-based EGDT, 18.2% with protocol-based standard therapy, and 18.9% with usual care; protocol-based care versus usual care RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.82–1.31; p=0.83).
shift_action: Follow the active local sepsis pathway. Do not place a central line solely to reproduce the original EGDT CVP or ScvO₂ targets.
review_note: The v3 numerical summary was accurate; treatment language was narrowed to the evidence tested by the trial.

title: ARISE
reference: ARISE Investigators and ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:1496–1506. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1404380
the_hook: A multinational randomized comparison of EGDT and usual care in adults presenting to emergency departments with early septic shock.
if_consultant_asks: EGDT did not reduce 90-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care and increased use of fluids, vasopressors, transfusion, and dobutamine during the intervention.
killer_stat: Ninety-day mortality was 18.6% with EGDT versus 18.8% with usual care (absolute risk difference −0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −4.1 to 3.6; p=0.90).
shift_action: Follow the active local sepsis pathway. Do not reproduce invasive EGDT targets as a mandatory bundle solely on the basis of the historical Rivers protocol.
review_note: Removed the v3 instruction to target early lactate clearance because ARISE tested EGDT versus usual care, not a universal lactate-clearance mandate.

title: ProMISe
reference: Mouncey PR et al. N Engl J Med. 2015;372:1301–1311. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1500896
the_hook: A pragmatic UK randomized trial with an integrated cost-effectiveness analysis comparing 6-hour EGDT with usual care.
if_consultant_asks: EGDT did not improve 90-day survival, increased treatment intensity and ICU use, and had a low probability of being cost-effective.
killer_stat: Ninety-day mortality was 29.5% with EGDT versus 29.2% with usual care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85–1.20; p=0.90).
shift_action: Follow the active local sepsis pathway; do not institute invasive EGDT monitoring solely to achieve CVP or ScvO₂ targets.
review_note: The v3 mortality figures were accurate. The display now links directly to the primary report.

title: Rivers Early Goal-Directed Therapy (EGDT)
reference: Rivers E et al. N Engl J Med. 2001;345:1368–1377. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa010307
the_hook: The single-centre trial that established early structured resuscitation as an influential concept in septic shock.
if_consultant_asks: The original EGDT protocol reduced mortality in its trial, but later multicentre ProCESS, ARISE, and ProMISe trials found no mortality benefit from mandatory EGDT targets over contemporary usual care.
killer_stat: Original in-hospital mortality was 30.5% with EGDT versus 46.5% with standard therapy (p=0.009).
shift_action: Treat this as historical evidence. Follow the current local sepsis protocol; do not place a central line solely to target CVP or ScvO₂ from the original EGDT bundle.
review_note: Removed the v3's unreferenced 20–30 mL/kg instruction and retained the later multicentre context.

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
the_hook: A randomized comparison of capillary-refill-time-targeted and lactate-targeted resuscitation strategies in early septic shock.
if_consultant_asks: The capillary-refill strategy did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality, although it was associated with less organ dysfunction at 72 hours.
killer_stat: Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34.9% with peripheral-perfusion targeting versus 43.4% with lactate targeting (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.55–1.02; p=0.06).
shift_action: Capillary refill can contribute to bedside perfusion assessment, but this trial alone did not establish it as a mortality-superior replacement for other targets. Follow the local shock protocol.
review_note: Corrected the v3 action, which treated a non-significant mortality trend as sufficient for a directive.

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2
reference: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Investigators. JAMA. 2025;334(22):1988–1999. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.20402
the_hook: A multicentre randomized trial of personalized hemodynamic resuscitation targeting capillary refill time versus usual care in early septic shock.
if_consultant_asks: The intervention was superior for a hierarchical composite of death, duration of vital support, and hospital length of stay, with the difference driven mainly by duration of vital support.
killer_stat: The primary hierarchical outcome favoured CRT-targeted personalized resuscitation (win ratio 1.16, 95% CI 1.02–1.33; p=0.04).
shift_action: Interpret the intervention as a structured personalized protocol, not a stand-alone instruction to titrate fluids or vasopressors from capillary refill alone. Use the locally approved shock pathway.
review_note: Replaced the v3's vague 'validated at scale' wording with the actual hierarchical endpoint and its main driver.

title: The BOUGIE Trial
the_hook: A pragmatic multicentre randomized comparison of bougie-first and stylet-first strategies for emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill adults.
if_consultant_asks: Routine bougie use did not significantly improve first-attempt success over a stylet in the trial population; the result does not address every difficult-airway scenario or rescue use after failure.
killer_stat: First-attempt success was 80.4% with bougie versus 83.0% with stylet (risk difference −2.6 percentage points, 95% CI −7.3 to 2.2; p=0.27).
shift_action: Choose the device according to the airway plan, anatomy, operator competence, and local difficult-airway protocol; do not infer universal superiority.
review_note: Corrected the v3 values of 80.5%, −2.5%, and its confidence interval to the published primary analysis.

title: RECOVERY: Dexamethasone in Hospitalized COVID-19
reference: RECOVERY Collaborative Group. N Engl J Med. 2021;384:693–704. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2021436
the_hook: An open-label randomized platform comparison of dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days versus usual care in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
if_consultant_asks: Dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality among patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation or oxygen at randomization, but not among patients receiving no respiratory support.
killer_stat: Mortality was 29.3% versus 41.4% in invasively ventilated patients (rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.51–0.81) and 23.3% versus 26.2% with oxygen alone (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.94).
shift_action: Use the current locally approved COVID-19 pathway and check contraindications and interacting indications; do not extrapolate benefit to patients who need no respiratory support.
review_note: The v3 subgroup figures were accurate; bedside wording was changed from a universal instruction to local-protocol use.

title: TRANSFER-AMI
reference: Cantor WJ et al. N Engl J Med. 2009;360:2705–2718. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa0808276
the_hook: A randomized comparison of routine early PCI and standard ischemia-guided care after fibrinolysis in high-risk STEMI patients presenting to non-PCI centres.
if_consultant_asks: A pharmacoinvasive strategy with transfer for PCI within 6 hours after fibrinolysis reduced the 30-day composite ischemic endpoint without a significant increase in major bleeding.
killer_stat: The 30-day composite endpoint occurred in 11.0% with routine early PCI versus 17.2% with standard treatment (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.87; p=0.004).
shift_action: Activate the regional STEMI and transfer pathway. Eligibility, fibrinolysis, rescue PCI, and transfer timing must follow the current local network protocol.
review_note: The v3 primary endpoint figures were retained and linked to the primary report; the action was scoped to an approved STEMI network.

title: STORM-PE
reference: Lookstein RA et al. Circulation. 2026;153:21–34. doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.077232
the_hook: A 100-patient randomized comparison of computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy plus anticoagulation versus anticoagulation alone for intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism.
if_consultant_asks: Thrombectomy produced a greater reduction in RV/LV ratio at 48 hours. The trial was small, used a surrogate efficacy endpoint, and did not establish a mortality or patient-centred outcome benefit.
killer_stat: Mean RV/LV ratio reduction was 0.52 with thrombectomy versus 0.24 with anticoagulation, a difference of 0.27 (95% CI 0.12–0.43; p<0.001); 7-day major adverse events were 4.3% versus 7.5% (p=0.681).
shift_action: Do not interpret STORM-PE as a mandate for routine thrombectomy. Use multidisciplinary PE risk assessment and the locally approved escalation pathway.
review_note: Corrected the v3 publication from 2025 to 2026 and removed the claim of proven clinical benefit; the primary efficacy measure was RV/LV ratio.

title: RENOVATE
reference: RENOVATE Investigators and BRICNet Authors. JAMA. 2025;333(10):875–890. doi:10.1001/jama.2024.26244
the_hook: A Bayesian noninferiority randomized trial of high-flow nasal oxygen versus face-mask noninvasive ventilation across five acute-respiratory-failure groups.
if_consultant_asks: HFNO met the prespecified noninferiority criterion for intubation or death at 7 days in four groups; the immunocompromised hypoxemic group stopped for futility, and findings in several groups were sensitive to model assumptions and small samples.
killer_stat: The trial enrolled 1,766 patients; noninferiority was declared in four of five prespecified patient groups using a posterior-probability threshold of at least 0.992 for an odds ratio below 1.55.
shift_action: Do not treat RENOVATE as evidence that HFNO is universally first-line or that escalation can be delayed. Select and monitor respiratory support under the local cause-specific pathway.
review_note: The v3 summary omitted the immunocompromised-group futility stop, noninferiority margin, and sensitivity caveats and made an unsupported universal first-line recommendation.

title: UK-ROX
the_hook: A pragmatic randomized comparison of conservative oxygen exposure and usual oxygen therapy in mechanically ventilated ICU adults.
if_consultant_asks: Targeting an SpO₂ of 90% (range 88%–92%) reduced oxygen exposure but did not significantly reduce 90-day all-cause mortality or improve major secondary outcomes.
killer_stat: Ninety-day mortality was 35.4% with conservative oxygen versus 34.9% with usual care (adjusted risk difference 0.7 percentage points, 95% CI −0.7 to 2.0; p=0.28).
shift_action: Do not adopt the v3's 90%–94% target or claim noninferiority from UK-ROX. Use the locally approved oxygen target for the patient's condition.
review_note: Critical correction: v3 described a noninferiority result and a 90%–94% target. UK-ROX tested superiority with a target of 90% (range 88%–92%) and was neutral.

title: THAPCA-OH
reference: Moler FW et al. N Engl J Med. 2015;372:1898–1908. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1411480
the_hook: A randomized comparison of targeted hypothermia at 33.0°C and targeted normothermia at 36.8°C in comatose children after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
if_consultant_asks: The trial did not find a statistically significant difference in 12-month survival with good neurobehavioral outcome. Both groups received active temperature control and fever prevention.
killer_stat: Good neurobehavioral survival at 12 months was 20% with hypothermia versus 12% with normothermia (relative likelihood 1.54, 95% CI 0.86–2.76; p=0.14).
shift_action: Use the current paediatric post-arrest temperature-control protocol. A non-significant result does not prove equivalence or justify abandoning active fever prevention.
review_note: Changed the v3's categorical 'does not provide benefit' wording to the trial's non-significant estimate and retained the importance of active temperature control.

title: RESOLVE
the_hook: A phase III randomized placebo-controlled trial of drotrecogin alfa in children with severe sepsis.
if_consultant_asks: Drotrecogin alfa did not improve the composite organ-failure endpoint. Overall serious bleeding was similar, while CNS bleeding was numerically higher with treatment, particularly among infants younger than 60 days.
killer_stat: Serious bleeding during 28 days was 6.7% with drotrecogin alfa versus 6.8% with placebo (p=0.97); CNS bleeding was 4.6% versus 2.1% (p=0.13).
shift_action: Historical evidence only: drotrecogin alfa was withdrawn from the market and is not a current sepsis treatment. Follow the current paediatric sepsis protocol.
review_note: Corrected the v3 claim of a significant overall bleeding increase; the overall rate was similar and the CNS-bleeding difference was not statistically significant.

title: PROFILE
reference: Noor NM et al. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024;9(5):415–427. doi:10.1016/S2468-1253(24)00034-7
the_hook: A multicentre biomarker-stratified randomized comparison of top-down infliximab plus an immunomodulator versus accelerated step-up treatment in newly diagnosed active Crohn's disease.
if_consultant_asks: Top-down treatment markedly increased sustained steroid-free and surgery-free remission, but the prognostic biomarker did not show clinical utility or identify differential treatment benefit.
killer_stat: Sustained steroid-free and surgery-free remission to week 48 occurred in 79% with top-down therapy versus 15% with accelerated step-up care (absolute difference 64 percentage points, 95% CI 57–72; p<0.0001); biomarker–treatment interaction p=0.944.
shift_action: This is specialist disease-management evidence, not an emergency-department instruction. Treatment choice requires gastroenterology assessment, shared decision-making, and the current local formulary and guideline.
review_note: Critical correction: v3 claimed the biomarker stratified high-risk patients for benefit. PROFILE found no biomarker–treatment interaction; the top-down strategy benefit was not biomarker-dependent.
